title: Israel president asks opposition leader Eisenkot to form government
description: Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with
body: Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension."Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision.Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said.The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.The election results had implied three possible options for the formation of a government: a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached.He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult.There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two.During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled".In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

schema.headline: Israel president asks opposition leader Eisenkot to form government

title: 'Please take the job!' - Trump asks UFC boss Dana White to be White House press secretary
description: US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post."Da
body: US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post."Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Dana, please take the job!"It's unclear whether the president's public job offer is genuine. The BBC has asked the White House and UFC, along with its parent company TKO Group Holdings, for comment.The vacancy for White House press secretary has been open since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia exited after just a few days on the job.Trump's post comes after his fellow Republicans were routed in the US midterm elections, losing their congressional majorities.In Saturday afternoon's post, Trump called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked that he bring a number of high-profile UFC fighters with him on the job "even though some are not from our Country"."We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote, alongside photos of the six fighters. Following Trump's post, White posted an Instagram photo of himself behind the lectern in the White House press briefing room. "On to the next chapter," White's post said, though it was unclear if the post was tongue-in-cheek. White, who is also the chief of Zuffa Boxing, was ringside for a fight in London on Saturday between British former world champion Chris Billam-Smith and Jamaican-born Briton Cheavon Clarke at the Copper Box Arena.The BBC was trying to reach him for comment.Famously combative, White has at times clashed with journalists covering the sport during news conferences.In 2020, he released a video targeting reporters who had questioned the UFC's decision to hold fights early in the pandemic.In 2009, he released an expletive-laden video tirade using an anti-gay slur while rebutting a journalist's story about changes to backstage credentialing rules at UFC events.White is a longtime ally - and friend - of Trump.When White and his business partners bought the then-struggling UFC organisation for $2m in 2001, the sport was facing intense bipartisan backlash.Just five years earlier, Republican Senator John McCain had famously labelled mixed martial arts "human cockfighting", sparking bans in 36 US states."None of the venues wanted [the UFC]," White told CBS, the BBC's US partner, in 2025. "They didn't believe in it. They didn't like it, and they were worried about the type of crowd that would show up for this type of event."With mainstream arenas shutting them out, White credits Trump with saving the organisation by hosting two UFC events at the Trump Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 2001.This summer, the UFC held a cage match on the White House lawn.White became a speaker for Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.It is far from clear whether he would have the time to take on the role of White House press secretary, one of the most gruelling jobs in the political arena.White already has a number of time-consuming commitments.As well as leading UFC and Power Slap, a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, he just launched Zuffa Boxing, a professional promotion company.And last year he was unveiled as one of three new board members of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

schema.headline: 'Please take the job!' - Trump asks UFC boss Dana White to be White House press secretary

title: Veterans shouldn't sleep rough this Christmas, Burnham says
description: No one who served in the UK armed forces should have to sleep on the streets this Christmas, Andy Burnham has said. Downing Street said the prime mini
body: No one who served in the UK armed forces should have to sleep on the streets this Christmas, Andy Burnham has said. Downing Street said the prime minister will personally write to councils across England on Armistice Day (11 November) to urge them to draw up specific plans to offer accommodation for veterans sleeping rough ahead of the festive period.He will say that, going forward, national and local government should work under the "simple principle" that "no one who has served our country should ever be left to sleep rough on our streets".Burnham will ask local authorities to use part of the additional £874m already announced to tackle homelessness specifically for housing veterans."People who stepped forward prepared to put their lives on the line for the rest of us should never lack a roof over their head," Burnham said in a statement issued on Saturday. "When they need help, the country owes them more than warm words. It owes them a bed every night, a proper plan and someone in their corner from day one."The PM will ask councils to work with local organisations and charities to tackle homelessness amongst veterans.Downing Street said an additional £8.7m in funding would be allocated to eight organisations across the UK to help housing providers offer assistance to veterans with complex needs, including those with health or addiction problems.Among them are Veteran Housing Scotland, Launchpad and SSAFA, the Armed Forces Charity.The pledge, announced ahead of Remembrance Sunday, is part of Burnham's wider plan to offer everyone currently sleeping rough a bed this winter.The most recent official figures estimated that there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England - a record high. The number of people recorded as sleeping rough has been on the rise since 2021.The government has committed £4.4bn in total to end rough sleeping.Burnham previously faced criticism from the Conservatives for failing to end rough sleeping while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester. He argued that Manchester's scheme attracted rough sleepers from the surrounding regions, adding that "it's only if everywhere does it at the same level that you can actually end rough sleeping".Liberal Democrats defence spokesman James MacCleary MP said the funding was an "important first step" but that "a one-off cash injection won't fix a crisis years in the making".He urged Burnham to guarantee long-term funding for councils to tackle homelessness "for good" and to put in place measures to prevent veterans "falling through the cracks in the first place".The prime minister is urging any veterans who are sleeping rough, or those supporting them, to call a UK-wide helpline on 0800 9520774 to be connected directly to housing and other specialist support.

schema.headline: Veterans shouldn't sleep rough this Christmas, Burnham says

title: Nottingham Forest 3-1 Man City: Enzo Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare
description: Enzo Maresca left the City Ground on Saturday evening with chants of "can we play you every week?" ringing in his ears - and the Italian's dream start
body: Enzo Maresca left the City Ground on Saturday evening with chants of "can we play you every week?" ringing in his ears - and the Italian's dream start as Manchester City manager is rapidly turning into a nightmare.Amid a sea of noise from the home faithful on the banks of the River Trent, the delirious Forest supporters witnessed their side produce a thrilling performance as City sunk to a third straight Premier League loss.Maresca's leaky backline continues to make defensive blunders and once Josko Gvardiol gave the ball away for Jair Cunha to open the scoring in the sixth minute, City were on the back foot.With Arsenal edging past Hull earlier in the day and keeping another clean sheet, City head into the international break searching for answers after a 3-1 loss and six points behind the champions.Maresca said: "The first half we didn't match [Forest's] intensity or win duels or second balls. The first thing required in these games is intensity."We tried to react at 2-0 but it's too late. We scored one, probably could have scored more but in transition we concede one more. No panic. We need to understand but no panic."Asked why the intensity was low, Maresca replied: "I need to analyse that."The situation already looks bleak for City, but what does history show?Should Brighton fail to beat Brentford on Sunday, Arsenal would be just the fourth side in Premier League history to have a six-point lead after 10 games, while only two teams have been so far behind as City at this stage and gone on to win the title.One of those was Manchester United in 2002-03. The other? City themselves in 2013-14 under Manuel Pellegrini.But Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton have the opportunity to leap up to second place and five points behind the Gunners should they beat Brentford.There is another factor which looms large over City's campaign.The club have lodged an appeal after being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules.That process is ongoing - and it is not yet known what potential sanctions City could face.But - even if any possible punishment does not affect this season - their title hopes are looking slimmer by the match.With his hands tucked inside his trouser pockets and his head bowed, a forlorn-looking Maresca paced the touchline towards the end of the match.The City boss said during the week he was still getting to know his players, but performances like the one against Forest will provide some clarity as to who he can, and cannot, trust.After starting the season with seven straight wins, City have hit real trouble with defeats against Aston Villa, Brighton and now a pumped-up Forest.Their problems at the back are not helping as it was another game where individual errors cost them dearly - and former striker Liam Delap took full advantage of the lapses in concentration with two goals.Gvardiol was at fault for the first, Iliman Ndiaye and Elliot Anderson got in a muddle for the second, while Matheus Nunes did not put a challenge in for the third."Before the game all the talk was about individual errors," former Forest winger Steve Stone told BBC Radio 5 Live. "Apart from the first goal, this hasn't been about that - the line is disjointed."The full-backs were very wide. If the ball turns over quickly and you pass it with your first pass you can be right through them. They have been exposed today. "Oliver Glasner's team have played through them every time."It was a miserable return to the City Ground for Anderson since his £116m move to City in the summer and the midfield dynamic alongside Enzo Fernandez does not seem to be working.The Argentine should have scored with a headed chance from close range but spent much of the game complaining in referee Sam Barrott's ear - City team-mates and supporters may be expecting more from their club record signing.The former Chelsea player scored in the midweek Champions League win at RB Leipzig, but that is his only goal or assist in his past nine games.Maresca needs to work out how to get the best out of Fernandez during the international break.Stone added: "I came here tonight thinking City would win, I thought they had chances. This is a real hammer blow to them, there is something not right about the back four at the minute."I have never seen a City team give the ball away so much in the middle of the park."Rayan Cherki's stunning strike gave City hope but they could not turn it around and the numbers following the result make for grim:City have lost three consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run of four in November-December 2024They have become the second team in English top-flight history - after Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05 - to win their first seven games of a season and then lose their next threeThis was their first league defeat by two or more goals against a side starting the day in the relegation zone since November 2008 (a 2-0 loss to Bolton Wanderers).Maresca was forced to chop and change his defence again, withdrawing both Gvardiol and Marc Guehi at half-time because of injuries, according to the manager.It meant Nunes came in at right-back, with Abdukodir Khusanov moving inside, and Nico O'Reilly playing down the left.Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport: "I thought City's performance was poor in terms of mentality."To make so make so many mistakes when you go anywhere in the Premier League, but especially to a team who are fighting for the lives, and you know they're going to come after you."They were sloppy with the ball, not winning duels. I would even probably go as far as saying there was probably a bit of arrogance at the start of the game from them. "I think that there are now some big questions to ask the manager about how he gets them back on track. I think with the talent they have got, it is not going to be a big problem."But I think defensively, maybe sticking to the same backline for a little while is the way forward."

schema.headline: Nottingham Forest 3-1 Man City: Enzo Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare

title: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
description: A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, incl
body: A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict. On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military."We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

schema.headline: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme

title: New Zealand election: No clear winner after tight general election
description: Figure caption, New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?ByOlivia Ireland and Tiffanie TurnbullReporting fromWellingtonUpdated 7 hours
body: Figure caption, New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?ByOlivia Ireland and Tiffanie TurnbullReporting fromWellingtonUpdated 7 hours agoThere was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.Image source, EPAImage caption, New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon addressed supporters in Auckland as votes were being countedThe electoral commission was not due to announce the official result until 27 November.Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."Elsewhere, Labour leader Hipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground". More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share. But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern". "It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins speaking to supportersJulian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

schema.headline: New Zealand election: No clear winner after tight general election

title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier
description: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy B
body: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.He said there was not a "single market à la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms"."There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime. Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent £350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead". Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly £350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS". Critics have said that the £350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's £75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the £350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise. ​In his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only £175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the £350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

schema.headline: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier

title: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Monty Done! Monty and his dog, Ned, have been a fixture on the showByPaul GlynnCulture reporterTV hortic
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Monty Done! Monty and his dog, Ned, have been a fixture on the showByPaul GlynnCulture reporterTV horticulturalist Monty Don thanked viewers and his furry friend Ned the dog while presenting his final episode of Gardeners' World, after more than two decades on air.The head gardener on the long-running BBC TV series signed off from Longmeadow garden, where the show has been based for 16 years, on Friday."From myself, Ned, and Longmeadow it's the final goodbye," he said on the programme, adding it had been "a privilege and pleasure" to share his garden experiences with so many people.During the episode, Don, 71, confirmed he would remain part of the presenting line-up for next year's Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Chelsea Flower Show.Image caption, Monty Don started on Gardeners' World in 2003, replacing Alan TitchmarshHe added he will feature in two winter specials, expected to air between now and Christmas.One celebratory episode will see him reflect on his years presenting the series and the changes he has seen at Longmeadow, external, which is also the garden of his private home, which he and his wife Sarah bought in 1991.'Good luck with your own gardens'Don replaced Alan Titchmarsh on the show in 2003, at his predecessor's request."I first began presenting Gardeners' World 23 years ago at Berryfields, and we came here to Longmeadow 16 years ago - in that time, things have changed," he recalled, on Friday's farewell."The garden has grown, Nigel has been and gone, and Nellie and Patty [his previous dogs], but there has been one constant factor, and that has been the incredible privilege and pleasure of sharing my garden and my gardening life with you here, as well as working with so many superb people."So, thank you. Thank you for coming on that journey with me and good luck with your own gardens in the future. So, for the last time... goodbye."Image source, BBC StudiosDetails of the next series of Gardeners' World will be announced at a later date, the BBC noted in a statement ahead of Don's farewell. His successor has not yet been named. Bookmakers and viewers have pointed to regular co-presenters like Frances Tophill and Adam Frost as top contenders, though Tophill has played down expectations of stepping directly into his shoes.Prior to fronting Gardeners' World, Don hosted other shows including Tomorrow's World, Holiday and - a preview of coming attractions - a gardening segment on This Morning.He took a three-year break from the programme after suffering a minor stroke in 2008.In September this year, Don announced that the current series would be his last. In a statement, he said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience", but added that "now is the right time for a change".The BBC said at the time that Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.Don was made an OBE by Queen Elizabeth, in 2018, for services to horticulture, broadcasting and charity. And he also received the RHS Victoria Medal of Honour - highest honour in horticulture.His final episode of Gardeners' World is available to stream now on BBC iPlayer.

schema.headline: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades

title: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teased in new photos
description: New images have been revealed ahead of the Christmas special of BBC series The Other Bennet Sister.Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the
body: New images have been revealed ahead of the Christmas special of BBC series The Other Bennet Sister.Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 6.5 million UK viewers in its first 28 days.The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn.Filming wrapped on the three-part Christmas special at the end of August.Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming episodes, but the BBC teased: "With marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs Hayward?" as fans eagerly await its return.The first series of The Other Bennet Sister focused on Mary, the oft-overlooked middle sister in Pride and Prejudice, as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England where marriage is both an aspiration and a necessity.It was mostly filmed in south Wales at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys.The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, also primarily in Wales.Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones returns to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter.

schema.headline: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teased in new photos

title: What happens if the internet goes down? BlackSky - the UK's emergency backup plans
description: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong."I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everythin
body: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong."I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everything went off," the professor at Lancaster University told the BBC. "Streetlights were off. The sodium glow that we can see over the horizon from Morecambe was off." The next day he went for a walk."[It was] almost like a zombie movie," he said. "People trying to find phone reception, wondering where things were, and there was a huge queue at the one working telephone box."At 22:45 on 5 December 2015, the River Lune - which flows directly through Lancaster - had flooded, and the electricity supply to 61,500 people in the city went.Households lost light and heat, some water supplies also began to fail because they relied on electric pumps. The railway station closed. So too petrol stations and shops. Most cash machines didn't work. Traffic lights failed.The two communication systems that survived were copper wire landline telephones and FM radio. The local commercial radio station The Bay had an emergency generator and one landline and a reporter was sent outside the affected area to ring in with information.Three months later, Kemp, a professor of engineering with a specialism in safety and electrical systems, gathered people together to look at everything that had gone wrong."It is perhaps ironic that, in a society with huge commitment to digital infrastructure, the most reliable source of news was a commercial station using technology that would have been familiar to the engineers on the 1960s Radio Caroline pirate radio ship," the subsequent report concluded. For Kemp and others in the field of civil contingency, Lancaster was a warning. When a town loses power for several days, our connected world falls apart. This kind of disruption has been given a name: a Black Sky event. At a recent summit on UK resilience, the conversation focused on the need for the UK to be able to withstand a Black Sky event for a minimum of 72 hours. "We are nine meals from anarchy" is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.The much talked about "Be Ready" campaign is designed to help ready us for all sorts of possible crises, but the government says there is no specific threat to the grid. Regardless, a Black Sky event is definitely at the backs of people's minds.In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan. Only a small number of staff know the full details, but from what I have gleaned, about 100 people in the BBC will run a special emergency radio studio. It will have secure lines of communication not dependent on the internet, and fuel, water and food to ensure it can operate without resupply for at least three days.This emergency service will broadcast pre-arranged government messaging. The scripts have already been published online., external They include instructions on how much people should be drinking each day and how to dispose of toilet waste without flushing the toilet.Other information will be broadcast via satellite vehicles from a select number of journalists at emergency centres around the UK, which will carry on as long as the diesel lasts.The BBC's broadcasts will be sent via radio transmission towers, isolated from the internet and equipped with tanks of between five and 40,000 litres (8,800 gallons) of diesel to keep their generators going for three days - FM radio is power hungry. The teams will be using satellite phones to keep in touch and if these stop working there are pre-agreed protocols and meet-up points.Why FM? Because it works almost everywhere, even in a blackout or a crippling cyber-attack."It was originally thought we should plan for five to seven days," I was told quietly by one BBC insider. "The latest advice from Neso [National Energy System Operator] is that they will probably be able to get the power back on in two to three days."Of course, fears of a grid failure are not new, but recent events such as the mass blackout in Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 have pushed it up the agenda. And the more it happens, the more it reveals the problems it can create in our networked world.People need to know power cuts are about more than just the lights going out, says Lord Harris, chair of the UK's National Preparedness Commission. ''It's likely to stop the water supply because unless you happen to be located neatly downstream of a reservoir, that requires electricity," he told me.More importantly, sewage tends to solidify unless water can move through it, he adds, "and that then causes blockages, the whole thing backs up, you get sewage flowing out, flowing back up the system".It's common for governments in Europe to regularly advise households to stock up on supplies in case of a national emergency - but the UK is behind in its warnings to the population. However, work has begun on some backup systems, such as High Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS). The government is spending £70m developing planes that can circle over the UK and provide at least a week of emergency mobile phone and internet connectivity at times of crisis. "When ground networks fail, there are limits to what satellites can provide as a fallback," said Rico Chandra, programme director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms, the company developing HAPS plans.  We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails. In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications". However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".The Cabinet Office said: "The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid's 75-year history."Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour. The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.The response from the government was that while  copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused."If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.It felt like an omen.

schema.headline: What happens if the internet goes down? BlackSky - the UK's emergency backup plans

title: Arsenal 1-0 Hull City: Another 1-0 for relentless Arsenal - but did Martin Odegaard spare VAR blushes?
description: It was not pretty, but Martin Odegaard's goal was enough to secure the 1-0 win that ensured Arsenal go into the international break as the Premier Lea
body: It was not pretty, but Martin Odegaard's goal was enough to secure the 1-0 win that ensured Arsenal go into the international break as the Premier League leaders.It was Arsenal's 34th 1-0 win under Mikel Arteta, to equal their best start to a Premier League season under the Spaniard of 27 points earned after 10 games in 2022-23.No team has enjoyed more 1-0 wins since Arteta was appointed back in 2019, with the Gunners winning their past 10 home games in all competitions, keeping eight clean sheets in that time.Odegaard's goal though, bundled home from close range, may well have been a relief to those at Pro Ref, too.A controversial video assistant referee (VAR) decision, which denied the Gunners a first-half penalty, threatened to be the story as a largely uneventful game drifted by.When referee Farai Hallam was sent to the pitchside monitor for a VAR review for a shirt pull by Nobel Mendy on Kai Havertz, surely everyone inside the Emirates was expecting a penalty.The irony would not be lost on Liverpool fans, who were denied a VAR penalty for a shirt pull last weekend when Arsenal's Jurrien Timber tugged back Alexander Isak.Unlike Isak, Havertz made sure everyone - including VAR Michael Oliver, was aware that a defender had hold of his shirt.Indeed, the cheers had already begun when Hallam started to describe the foul to the crowd - but Gunners supporters were stopped in their tracks. The referee pivoted to an offside against Havertz, and play restarted with a free-kick to Hull.Had Arsenal not mustered that 72nd-minute winner from their captain, much of the attention would, once again, have been on VAR.If Arsenal had dropped points, it wouldn't have been the first time this weekend that a match would have been dominated by discussions about the video officials.On Friday, Coventry City were denied what appeared to be a clear penalty against Everton for a hair pull by James Tarkowski on Caleb Yirenkyi. Then in the second half, when Thierno Barry scored to put the Toffees 2-1 up and the ball appeared to come off his hand.The controversy continued in Saturday's early kick-off between Leeds and Tottenham. First, Leeds wanted a penalty for handball by Mateus Fernandes, though replays did show the ball hit the Spurs player's shoulder.Then came the potential red card for a challenge by Jayden Bogle on Mathys Tel, which has split opinion. The VAR, Tony Harrington, eventually decided after a four-minute VAR check that the foul did not have enough force.That Tel was forced off injured, and referee John Brooks did not even show a yellow card on the field, only added to the frustration for Tottenham.So on to the Emirates, and again the debate was around VAR.It's a situation few would question. After all, an offside player winning a penalty surely goes against the very logic of the law?If an offside player is running to the ball and is fouled before they attempt to play the ball or challenge an opponent, then the foul is considered to come before the offside offence.The law seeks to prevent situations whereby defenders have carte blanche to foul attackers, just because the opponent is offside.But is a complex area of law and is very much open to interpretation.We have a few past case studies.In February 2019, the season before VAR came in, an offside Harry Kane was awarded a late penalty in a north London derby after being dragged down by Shkodran Mustafi.Two years ago, Newcastle were awarded a spot-kick against Bournemouth through a VAR intervention when Adam Smith tugged back an offside Fabian Schar.Yet last December, after being awarded a penalty against Leeds, Brentford's Dango Ouattara was ruled to be offside and the spot-kick ruled out through VAR.So which interpretation is correct? Kane and Schar, or Havertz and Ouattara?Ouattara was somewhat different, as he appeared to be engaging with Gabriel Gudmundsson as the ball was played.The Havertz example is more like the one involving Schar, who was running forward when his shirt was tugged back.But there is an additional consideration, and this is where Oliver's thinking will lie.Officials are asked to consider the likelihood of the attacker becoming involved in the play from a second phase. Let's say the ball could be first played by a team-mate, which then makes them onside. Then they are not purely benefitting from being offside.In the case of Schar and Kane, they could have benefitted from that second phase.Havertz was the only attacker who had any chance of being involved in the play, so the VAR determined offside was the fair outcome.Confused? You've got every right to be.At least tonight most of the talk will be about another victory for Arsenal - and not VAR.Another game, another win but still Arsenal are looking for their attack to spark into life.At the end of the day results matter but Arsenal, despite being top, are the lowest scorers of the teams in the top four.They have the best defence in the league and arguably Europe but goals are also seeming hard to come by at the other end.Arsenal have not scored more than twice in the league since the opening day of the season, when they put three past Coventry.Arteta's side are missing talisman Bukayo Saka, who is out with a quadricep injury, and has a unique partnership with Ben White and Martin Odegaard on the right.On the left Christos Tzolis started the season well but, after a hamstring injury while playing for Greece, the 24-year-old has not looked the same threat.The same can be said for Kai Havertz too.The 27-year-old picked up a hamstring injury playing for Germany and, even though he scored the winner against Liverpool, his performances have not reached the same level.Viktor Gyokeres is firmly second choice this season and Arteta is still working out how to get the best out of the maverick Eberechi Eze, while Noni Madueke is working to fill the gap left by Saka.Arteta was asked about the number of single-goal wins this season and what he can do to improve that."To be more efficient," was the answer the Gunners boss gave. "We are one against one against the keeper. That's happened twice today."There is a penalty there, there is another situation inside the box where the ball is bouncing. So many shots that have been deflected, blocked. We need to find ways to be more efficient, sometimes even more pragmatic."Sometimes my feeling is that we are trying to score a perfect goal against these low blocks. We need to be much more chaotic than that, and that's it. And open, I think, score much earlier because obviously that's going to change the course of the game." Even if the Gunners could be more free-flowing going forward, they have started the season in a formidable way - winning nine of their 10 league games.And if they manage to keep up that rate of winning, the Gunners will likely defend their Premier League crown and win back-to-back titles for the first time in 100 years.

schema.headline: Arsenal 1-0 Hull City: Another 1-0 for relentless Arsenal - but did Martin Odegaard spare VAR blushes?

title: Three held after boy hurt in sword attack near Gloucester school
description: Two men arrested after boy injured in sword attackImage source, PAImage caption, Police attended St Peter's High School in Tuffley, Gloucester, at 08:
body: Two men arrested after boy injured in sword attackImage source, PAImage caption, Police attended St Peter's High School in Tuffley, Gloucester, at 08:50 GMT on FridayByKirsten RobertsonWest of EnglandUpdated 8 hours agoTwo men and a boy have been arrested after a teenager was injured in an attack involving a sword near two schools in Gloucester.St Peter's High School and Willow Primary Academy, in Tuffley, were put into lockdown after the incident at 08:50 GMT on Friday. Police said a 17-year-old suffered a wound "believed to have been caused by the sword". A 19-year-old was arrested overnight on suspicion of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. An 18-year-old was held on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. Meanwhile another 17-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.The trio - who are all from Gloucester - remain in police custody for questioning.Two men, one with a sword, had been seen chasing two boys, according to police on Friday.Armed officers attended the scene to search for the suspects who reportedly fled on foot.Police said the 17-year-old suffered a "superficial wound believed to have been caused by the sword". The other boy involved was not injured.Image caption, The incident happened close to two Gloucester schoolsGloucestershire Police also said a woman who had previously been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender had been released on police bail.At the school gates outside St Peter's High School on Friday, a pupil called Jimmy told the BBC the situation was "really scary" and that they had been told to lock doors and turn lights off."At the time I was scared. My heart was racing," he said.Jimmy said pupils were locked in their classrooms for several hours.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Gloucestershire

title: NZ election: Can a new government win over disillusioned voters?
description: New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather."It's pret
body: New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather."It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread.""Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits."I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confessed. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explained, declining to chat further. "Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions. A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate. But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party – the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic. Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to:  finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs. But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview."It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened."The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries – set by a supermarket duopoly – is among the highest in the developed world.And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July."There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.Increasingly polarised public debate – around topics like Māori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration – have added to the mental load for many in those communities."There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day – a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia."It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity."It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young poeple - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts."There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.

schema.headline: NZ election: Can a new government win over disillusioned voters?

title: Married at First Sight UK: Relief, tears and sadness - how cast reacted to Channel 4 show being axed
description: Figure caption, Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegationsByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentUpdated 11:31 GMT"I'm delighted and so reli
body: Figure caption, Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegationsByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentUpdated 11:31 GMT"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after BBC Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.Image source, Married at First Sight UK, CPL ProductionsImage caption, Shona Manderson appeared on the 2023 series of Married at First Sight UKShona Manderson told me by telephone her main feeling was relief that their voices had been heard."Speaking out wasn't easy, but knowing that our voices have helped bring about change makes it all worthwhile," she said.Over the day, more MAFS UK cast members were in touch with us.Several were pleased by the decision to scrap the series, but others said it did not go far enough and called for more accountability.One cast member, who asked to remain anonymous, said people watching at home do not always appreciate this "isn't simply a television show" for those taking part."These are real people, real emotions."Image source, Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for SXSW LondonImage caption, April Banbury took part in the 2022 series of MAFS UKOthers we spoke to felt the show should have been taken off-air sooner.They include April Banbury, who took part in the 2022 series and whose on-screen husband was subsequently arrested on suspicion of controlling and coercive behaviour. The police investigation against him was later dropped, and her partner called the allegations against him "false"."I'm glad MAFS has been cancelled. It should have happened years ago," Banbury told us. "We want answers, we want those responsible to be held accountable, and we want to know how this was allowed to happen in the first place,” added another cast member, who asked to remain anonymous. He was echoed by Lia Perin, Partner at Taylor Hampton and lawyer for a number of MAFS UK participants.“Cancelling the show may prevent future harm, but it does not resolve questions about the treatment of previous contestants,” she told the BBC."Channel 4 owes them answers, not simply assurances that lessons have been learned."Image source, Lara EyreImage caption, Lara Eyre was a bride on the 2022 seriesOthers writing on social media said their experiences had been more positive, and that they were sad to see it go.Jay Howard, from the 2023 series, external, said the show had brought her friendships and opportunities, while Marilyse Corrigan, a 2021 bride, external, said it was a chapter of her life she looked back on "with fond memories".A number of cast members we spoke to also expressed concern for staff who had been working on the show, as well as sorrow for fans.Lara Eyre, who appeared on the 2022 series, told me she felt we were now "on the edge of a curb on how we treat reality TV stars and safeguarding", adding it was a "real shame" for those who filmed this year's series, which will never be aired, as well as a shame for fans of the show."I know a lot of people loved it, I loved it," she said.“Yes, I know it was traumatic, for sure, and there was a lot of bad things that went with the good. But it was a big part of a lot of people's lives, so it's sad it's not going to be on any more, but I also think this could've been avoided."Where does this go from here?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Channel 4's office in central LondonAs the dust settles, there are still many questions. Only "a summary of findings" from Channel 4’s review has been released, rather than the full report.We still do not know what the broadcaster did when it was first warned about the serious allegations by the production company.Why did it take them so long to investigate? And why did they only do so once BBC Panorama raised the alarm?We put some of these questions to Channel 4's boss Priya Dogra on Thursday. She said the broadcaster's handling of incidents as they arose was appropriate, and that the review had borne that out.In a statement to BBC News on Friday, Channel 4 said its review “did not seek to adjudicate on the serious allegations of wrongdoing against a small number of past contributors highlighted by Panorama, as those allegations remain a matter for the relevant authorities”.The Dark Side of Married at First SightPanorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.Watch on iPlayer nowIt said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom’s broadcasting code.Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee on 17 November, so we may hear more then.Either way, this is not the end of the story. There is an ongoing Ofcom investigation into the show - and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.The decision to scrap MAFS UK will also inevitably raise questions about what happens with the wider Married at First Sight format.If one broadcaster says the show has “run its course,” then those global versions may also come under the spotlight.Channel 4 has already said it will not be showing international editions like MAFS Australia again.And for the TV industry more broadly, questions will once again be asked about reality TV - and whether shows like this can ever keep their contributors safe.If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.ukGet in touchWhat is your reaction to the cancellation of MAFS UK? Get in touch.
